title: Artifact Recognition
subtitle: Eyes, muscles, movement and environment can win the game
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating artifact recognition within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain artifact recognition without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in artifact recognition.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to artifact recognition.

sections.explainSimply: Blinking, jaw tension, movement, sweat and electrical noise can look like changes in EEG.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Artifacts may be systematically rewarded if they move the trained metric in the desired direction. Clinicians need live raw-signal monitoring and behavioural observation.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Artifact handling includes prevention, channel monitoring, rejection rules and post-session review. Overcorrection can also remove genuine neural activity.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Trying to tune a faint radio station: contact, interference and antenna placement determine what reaches the speaker.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand artifact recognition to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: If the learner can raise the score by clenching, the protocol is training clenching.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using artifact recognition predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: If the learner can raise the score by clenching, the protocol is training clenching. Evidence classification: established signal-quality requirement.
